clue.text: It may be used to escape hazard from food that's fried at high temperature

definitions.text: It may be used to escape hazard

blocks.note: chips are fried potato strips
something at a high temperature is hot

explanation.surface: A cook escaping danger from a deep fryer running far too hot.
explanation.walkthrough: The hazard is a golf hazard such as a bunker or water, not a kitchen danger.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a short lofted stroke is played to lift the ball out of or over a hazard.

clue.text: Measure of persistent radioactivity in lithium or iron?

blocks.note: surface reading: a physics term for how long a radioactive substance keeps decaying
setter's reading: the chemical symbols Li and Fe are each one of the two halves of a four-letter word for existence

explanation.surface: A physicist wondering how long lithium or iron stays radioactive.
explanation.walkthrough: Li and Fe are the chemical symbols; put together they spell the word for being alive, so each one is a half of it, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A half-life is the time taken for half the atoms of a radioactive isotope to decay, the standard measure of its persistence.

clue.text: Like some leaders in power, not suitable for offices

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for power in physics
land zoned for homes is not meant for office buildings

explanation.surface: Some powerful leaders are dismissed as unfit to hold office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offices' suggests political posts, but the wordplay means office buildings, as in planning zones.
explanation.definitionFit: Heads of state in republics such as the USA are presidents, so their style of leadership is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Bird circles in two places in anticipation

indicators.note: says the round shapes are slotted inside the other word at two separate points

blocks.note: two circles look like two letter Os
hope is anticipation of something good

explanation.surface: A bird flies in circles over two spots, as if expecting something.
explanation.walkthrough: One O goes after the first two letters of HOPE and the other after the P, giving HOOPOE.
explanation.definitionFit: The hoopoe is a crested Eurasian bird with a distinctive call, a standard species name.

clue.text: Make heavy demands on island transport for hire

blocks.note: to tax someone is to strain them
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Islanders' transport for hire is under heavy strain.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab is a vehicle with a driver that carries paying passengers on request.

clue.text: For example, Marx family members as comrades

blocks.note: first meaning: Groucho, Harpo and Chico were the Marx siblings
second meaning: fellow members of a movement or union addressed as kin

explanation.surface: The Marx family pictured as fellow revolutionaries, with a nod to Karl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marx' points the reader to Karl and communism, but the family is the comedy team of the films.
explanation.definitionFit: Male siblings share parents, and the same word is used for trade-union or political comrades.

clue.text: Starts from airport somewhere in Africa, lands in East

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these four words

explanation.surface: A flight leaves an African airport and touches down in the East.
explanation.definitionFit: The continent covering most of the eastern lands of the world, from the Middle East to Japan.

clue.text: Person making judgment in court leading to outcry, so to speak?

definitions.text: Person making judgment in court leading to outcry, so to speak?

blocks.clueFragment: Person making judgment in court leading to outcry
blocks.note: surface reading: a judge whose courtroom ruling sparks public protest
setter's reading: the court is a tennis court and the cry is the official's shout that a ball has landed out

explanation.surface: A judge's controversial ruling provokes a public outcry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outcry' is split into an 'out' cry, the call made by the tennis official watching a line; 'so to speak' flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis this official watches a boundary and calls whether the ball landed in or out of play.

clue.text: Journalists king admitted to a current party activity

indicators.note: being admitted means let in, so these go inside the outer letters

blocks.note: taken as written
the press is journalists collectively
K is the chess abbreviation for king
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Reporters and a king are let into a fashionable party.
explanation.walkthrough: PRESS and K together go inside A ... I.
explanation.definitionFit: Après-ski is the socialising and partying that follows a day on the ski slopes.

clue.text: Ships, having lost little time, make run for it

indicators.note: something that has been lost is no longer there, so it is removed

blocks.note: a fleet is a group of ships
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Ships that are short of time make a dash to escape.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the final T from FLEET.
explanation.definitionFit: To run for it is to escape danger quickly, a synonym for running away.

clue.text: Worldly-wise type making epic that is so disorganised

indicators.note: something disorganised is in a muddle, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: all twelve letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A cultured person writes a sprawling, badly organised epic.
explanation.definitionFit: A sophisticate is a person of refined, worldly experience and taste.

clue.text: Like some races in angry state

blocks.note: cross means annoyed
a state is a nation

explanation.surface: Racial tension in a furious nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Races' suggests ethnic groups, but these are running races.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross-country races are run over open fields and rough ground rather than on a track.

clue.text: Don't object so much, stupid

definitions.note: read as two words, a verb phrase: mind less

blocks.note: first meaning: to object less
second meaning: thoughtless, without intelligence

explanation.surface: An impatient retort telling someone to stop complaining, ending in an insult.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words and it is an instruction to complain less.
explanation.definitionFit: Mindless describes acting without thought or intelligence, a close synonym for stupid.

clue.text: What's changed as result of cut in field

indicators.note: changed means altered, so the letters are put into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the letters of the word, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone asking what has changed after a cut was made in a field.
explanation.definitionFit: A swath is the strip or line of grass or crop laid down by one pass of a scythe or mower.

clue.text: For instance, I'm so absurdly following principle of self-interest

indicators.note: something done absurdly makes no sense, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: e.g. abbreviates the Latin for 'for example'
the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone admits to following a selfish creed in an absurd way.
explanation.definitionFit: Egoism is the ethical theory that self-interest is the proper basis of action.

clue.text: Person losing heart as lowly farm worker

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so its middle letters are dropped

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dispirited person working as a humble labourer on a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: The central RS of the six letters goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A peon is a Latin American agricultural labourer, a word for a lowly unskilled worker.

clue.text: Work by G&S that one plays

definitions.note: a noun phrase: a game one plays

blocks.note: first meaning: a comic opera by Gilbert and Sullivan
second meaning: a card game for a single player

explanation.surface: A Gilbert and Sullivan piece that one performs.
explanation.walkthrough: G&S is Gilbert and Sullivan, the Victorian comic-opera partnership; 'plays' suggests staging, but it means playing cards alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Patience is both the title of an 1881 operetta and the British name for the solo card game called solitaire in the US.

clue.text: Opportunity to learn about girl

blocks.note: c. abbreviates circa, Latin for about
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A chance to find out about a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A class is a lesson, a session in which students are taught.

clue.text: Something old king passed, making salad

blocks.note: Old King Cole of the nursery rhyme, with a possessive
something a ruler passes is a law

explanation.surface: An ancient monarch's decree somehow results in a salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something old king passed' reads as Old King Cole's law; Old King Cole is the merry old soul of the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleslaw is a salad of shredded raw cabbage and carrot dressed with mayonnaise.

clue.text: Darned partners embracing opponents

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so one pair wraps around the other

blocks.note: in bridge, South and North play as partners
East and West are the bridge pair facing North and South

explanation.surface: A couple hugging their rivals, with 'darned' as a mild curse.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge is played by two pairs named after compass points, so partners and opponents are compass letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To darn is to mend by sewing, so something darned has been stitched.

clue.text: Decisive defeat, later reviewed in court

indicators.note: a reviewed case is gone over again and rearranged, so the letters are reordered
says the rearranged word sits inside the other word

blocks.note: to court someone is to woo them
taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: A crushing loss is later examined in a law court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a courtroom, but it is the verb for romancing.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon's final defeat in 1815 gave the phrase 'meet one's Waterloo' for any decisive downfall.

clue.text: Short time in work on land brings excitement

indicators.note: places the short unit of time inside the farming word

blocks.note: hr is the abbreviation for hour
to till is to plough and work the soil

explanation.surface: A brief spell of farm work proves exhilarating.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrill is a sudden feeling of excitement and pleasure.

clue.text: Temperature inside dreadful lairs

indicators.note: tells us the single letter is put within the other word

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for temperature
hideous means dreadful

explanation.surface: It is horribly hot inside some awful dens.
explanation.definitionFit: Hideouts are hiding places, the dens or lairs of fugitives or animals.

clue.text: The writer is rising in academic field

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read upwards, so the order flips
places the flipped words inside the academic

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself: I am
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A writer climbing up the ranks within a scholarly discipline.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is the setter, so 'The writer is' becomes I AM.
explanation.definitionFit: A domain is an area of knowledge or activity, the same sense as a field of study.

clue.text: Novel in Welsh containing good sign for most British ladies

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into something fresh
the Welsh letters hold the extra letter within them before the shuffle

blocks.note: the letters of both words
G is the abbreviation for good
an omen is a sign of things to come

explanation.surface: A Welsh novel containing a hopeful portent for most women in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, but it is the signal to rearrange. Most British women live in England, which makes the definition fair.
explanation.definitionFit: England holds the majority of Britain's population, so most British women are women from England.

clue.text: Provoke attempt on a record, finally

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: a go is a try
taken as written
the closing letter of this word

explanation.surface: Taunting someone into finally trying for a record.
explanation.definitionFit: To goad is to urge or provoke someone, originally with a pointed stick used on cattle.

clue.text: Succinct refusal as customary behaviour

blocks.note: first meaning: the contraction of 'will not', a short way to say no
second meaning: one's habit or usual practice

explanation.surface: Someone habitually refuses things curtly.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the apostrophe: the contraction for 'will not' and the old noun for habit share letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Wont, as in 'as was his wont', is a noun for habitual practice; with an apostrophe it is a curt refusal.

clue.text: Piece of vital knowledge that's said to be cheap

definitions.note: an idiom-based description of the noun

indicators.note: a piece is a part, so the answer is a part of the words that follow

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An essential bit of know-how is dismissed as worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said' here belongs to the saying, not a sound clue; the proverb is that talk is cheap.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'talk is cheap' says words cost nothing compared with action, so this is the thing called cheap.

clue.text: Organiser of services in one of them

definitions.text: Organiser of services in one of them

blocks.note: surface reading: someone arranging services, apparently of the commercial or utility kind
setter's reading: religious services held in one of the armed services, the army, navy or air force

explanation.surface: A manager running one of the services they organise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Services' is used twice in two senses: church services and the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: A military clergyman leads worship and religious rites for troops in the forces.

clue.text: Lord who memorialised men in charge in 1854

definitions.text: Lord who memorialised men in charge in 1854

blocks.note: surface reading: a peer who commemorated some soldiers
setter's reading: the men were in the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava in 1854, not men in command

explanation.surface: A nobleman wrote a tribute to the officers in command in 1854.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In charge' looks like being in command, but it means taking part in the famous cavalry charge of the Crimean War.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson, the Poet Laureate, wrote 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' about the 1854 Balaclava disaster.
